messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bad Bayesian estimation in the Beta Power Distribution
parts:
Are you computing both with Stan so you know you have the
same model?

Bayesian estimates are posterior means, which can be arbitrarily
far away from the posterior mode, which is what you get from
the MLE. Often, asymptotically with more data, they'll converge
to the same value.

Why do you think that's a problem? What you want is not something
close to the MLE, but something that's well-calibrated to return
the parameters in the posterior intervals.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Bad Bayesian estimation in the Beta Power Distribution
parts:
> On Dec 8, 2016, at 2:12 PM, Bistoon <bistoon....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> OK. By below function, one can generate the Beta Power (BP) distribution in R:
>
> rBP = function(n, par) qbeta(runif(n),par[1],par[2])^(1/par[3])/par[4]
>
> Let me ask another question. If I generate n = 1000 observation from the BP, I expect that the BP will be a good fit (by using UMVUE, MRE, MLE, Bayes and etc.). Am I wrong?

"Bayes" isn't a specific estimation procedure. There are many ways
to define estimates with a Bayesian model. The usual way
to do it is as a posterior mean, as that minimizes expected
square error (posterior median minimizes expected absolute error).
This contrasts with the posterior mode you get with a MAP (or max
penalized likelihood) estimate. For a beta(a, b) distribution,
the posterior mode is (a - 1) / (a + b - 2) and the posterior mean
is a / (a + b). So if a/(a + b) remains constant and a and b
grow, they converge to the same place, but with less data, there's
no guarantee they'll even be close. Other skewed distributions
have similar problems. The MLE doesn't always exist, but the
Bayesian posterior mean will exist as long as the posterior has
finite variance.

How did you code that density in Stan? It looks like the normalization
might depend on the extra parameters.

- Bob

messages.author: 2d974991cab5f3a7
messages.subject: Re: Bad Bayesian estimation in the Beta Power Distribution
parts:
Thank you Bob. I use below code and define the log of BP distribution in target statement:

    data
        {
        int<lower=1> n;
        real<lower=0,upper=1> x[n];
        int<lower=0,upper=1> check;
        }
       
    parameters
        {
        real<lower=0> a;
        real<lower=0> b;
        real<lower=0> alpha;
        real<lower=0,upper=(1/max(x))> beta;
        }
   
    model
        {
        vector[2] s;
        if(check == 1)
            {
            a ~ gamma(1,.001);
            b ~ gamma(1,.001);
            alpha ~ gamma(1,.001);
            beta ~ uniform(0,1/max(x));
            }
        for(j in 1:2) s[j] = 0;
        for(i in 1:n)
            {
            s[1] = s[1] + log(x[i]);
            s[2] = s[2] + log1m(pow(x[i]*beta,alpha));
            }
        target += n*(log(alpha)+a*alpha*log(beta) - lbeta(a,b)) + (alpha*a-1)*s[1] + (b-1)*s[2];
        }

I attached the BP density again.

-Bistoon
